chapters.title: Intros and agenda
chapters.gist: Small talk about the Pacific Northwest and peak season, intros for Asher and Elena, and Tom sets a no-demo, discovery-only agenda.

chapters.title: Dispatch today: spreadsheets, overtime and chargebacks
chapters.gist: Marcus describes nightly spreadsheet routing for 420 trucks, overtime at about 14% of driver hours against a 6% target, and roughly $40k/month in late-delivery chargebacks; success would be dispatchers home by seven, overtime under 8% and chargebacks halved.

chapters.title: Systems, integrations and security
chapters.gist: Elena lays out Samsara telematics, a heavily customized 2014 on-prem Oracle TMS with no API, and requirements for Okta SSO, a SOC 2 Type II report and a 180-question security questionnaire; Tom defers the deep integration question to Daniel.

chapters.title: Decision process, budget and RouteWise
chapters.gist: CFO Dana Whitfield signs off after a pilot on Harbor & Pine's own trucks, with a decision by Oct 30; budget is around $300k/yr if the numbers hold, and RouteWise is competing at about $52 per truck per month.

chapters.title: Live ETA sharing and next steps
chapters.gist: Marcus calls live ETA sharing a must-have; Tom says it is on the roadmap for this quarter while Asher hedges that it is still being scoped. The group books a Routing v3 demo with Daniel for Thursday Oct 1 and agrees on security, data and briefing follow-ups.

turns.t: Hey, there he is. Marcus, how are you doing?
Hey Tom. Good, good. Sorry, I'm like two minutes late, I had a dispatcher grab me in the hallway on the way back from the yard. Classic Tuesday.
No, totally fine. That's kind of the whole reason we're talking, right? Dispatchers grabbing you in hallways.
Ha. Yeah. You're not wrong.
Is Elena joining? I saw she accepted the invite.
She is, she's — oh, there she is. Elena, I think you're on mute.
Sorry. Yes. Hi. I was in another call that ran over, I'm here now.

Hi Elena, nice to meet you. So I've got Asher on with me as well. Asher runs product at Tandem. I figured since you all have a pretty specific setup, it'd be good to have him on early instead of me playing telephone back to the product team.
Hey everyone. Yeah, happy to be here. I mostly want to listen today, honestly. Tom's driving.
Hey Asher. Where are you guys based? Are you down in the Bay?
Asher's in Oakland, I'm actually in Portland, so I'm basically your neighbor. How's the weather up there in — you're in Tacoma, right?

Kent. Close enough, nobody outside Washington knows the difference. It's doing that thing where it's sunny for an hour and then it's just not. Which, honestly, for us is fine. Fall's when volume ramps up and I would rather not have snow on top of that. Snoqualmie Pass in December is its own meeting.
Yeah, I bet. Peak season's coming. When does it really kick in for you?

Mid-October, and then it just doesn't stop until like the second week of January. The retail customers start pulling inventory forward, everybody wants their stuff in the DCs before Black Friday, and then there's returns after Christmas. So, yeah. Good timing for this conversation. Or terrible timing, depending on how you look at it.

Ha, we'll try to make it good timing. So here's what I was thinking for today, and stop me if you want to go somewhere else. Thirty-ish minutes. I'd love to just understand how dispatch works for you today, where it's breaking, what Elena's world looks like on the systems side, and then how you'd want to evaluate something like this. I'm not going to do a demo today, and that's on purpose. If it makes sense, we'll set up a proper one with our engineering folks on your data. Sound okay?
Yeah, that works. I appreciate not getting a forty-slide deck, honestly. The last vendor did twenty minutes on their founding story.
Works for me.
Great. So Marcus, maybe start wherever's easiest. Walk me through a night in dispatch.

Sure. So, okay, the short version is we run 420 trucks. Mostly regional freight, LTL and some full truckload, Washington, Oregon, a little bit of Idaho. We've got three terminals, Kent, Portland and Spokane. And every night the dispatch team builds the next day's routes. In spreadsheets. I wish I was exaggerating. It's Excel, it's a handful of really smart people who have been doing it for fifteen years, and a lot of tribal knowledge about which dock at which DC is going to make you wait two hours if you show up at 6:05 instead of 5:55.
Right. How many people are building routes?

Nine dispatchers across the three terminals, plus two leads. And they start around, I want to say four in the afternoon, once the order cutoff hits, and on a bad night they're there till ten, eleven. Which, you know, they're salaried, so that's not my overtime number, but it's a burnout number. I lost a lead in Spokane in June and it took me three months to backfill.
Wow. Okay.
Sorry, quick one. Roughly how many stops does a truck do in a day? Just so I have the shape of it in my head.

Depends on the terminal. Kent and Portland, the LTL trucks, eight to fourteen stops, a lot of them are DCs and some industrial. Spokane is longer hauls, fewer stops, more miles. If you averaged it out across the whole fleet, call it ten stops a truck. So something like four thousand stops a night, give or take, across the three terminals. On a peak day more.
Okay, got it. Thanks.

And the thing is, they're good. Like, the routes aren't terrible. But they're built for the plan, right? And the plan's dead by 7 a.m. A truck goes down, a driver calls out, a DC pushes an appointment, and then it's phones and whiteboards and somebody re-sorting a spreadsheet at a stoplight. Not literally. Hopefully.
When a truck goes down mid-day, what actually happens? Like, who re-plans, and how?

The lead at that terminal. Mostly by gut. They'll pull up Samsara, look at who's closest, and call around. Hey, can you pick up these four stops on your way back. And the driver says yes, because they're nice people and they want the hours, and then they blow through their day, and that's my overtime problem.
Yeah, let's talk about that. What's overtime looking like?
So, it's — I literally had this number up this morning. It's about fourteen percent of driver hours. Fourteen, fifteen. Let's say fourteen, I'll get yelled at by finance if I round up.
Fourteen percent of total driver hours is overtime.

Of total hours, yeah. And our target internally, the number we actually budget for, is six. So we're more than double. And some of that's peak, sure, but it was eleven in the spring. It's not just a seasonal thing, it's been creeping for a year and a half.
And that's paid at time and a half, I assume.

Time and a half, yeah. And then there's the hours-of-service piece, which is the scarier one. If a driver hits their limit, we've got a truck sitting at a truck stop somewhere with somebody else's freight on it and a relief driver two hours away. That's happened. Twice in August.
Three times.
Three times. Thank you. Elena keeps me honest. She has the Samsara logs, I have my memory.
Ha. Okay. And then on the customer side, you mentioned DCs. I'm guessing there are chargebacks?

Oh, yeah. That's the one that gets Dana's attention. So most of our big shippers, the retail ones, they run on-time-in-full programs. You miss your appointment window at the DC, they fine you. It's a percentage of the invoice or a flat fee depending on the retailer, and some of them are, honestly, pretty aggressive about it. There's one big-box account where fifteen minutes late is the same as not showing up. We're running about forty thousand a month in late-delivery chargebacks right now.
Forty thousand a month.

Give or take. Some months it's thirty-five. September was worse, I haven't seen the final yet. And that's money that just disappears. There's no fighting most of them, we've tried, the retailers have all the leverage.
Do you have a sense of how much of that is the plan being bad versus things going wrong during the day?

That's a great question and the honest answer is no, not really. My gut says it's like half and half. Some of it is we just build a route that was never going to make a 6 a.m. window at a DC, because the dispatcher forgot that dock is always backed up on Tuesdays, or they stacked too many stops before it. And some of it is the truck broke down at nine and nobody re-planned fast enough, so the 2 p.m. appointment at the other end of the route just quietly dies.
Okay. That's helpful. That split matters a lot for what we'd actually try to fix first. The nightly plan is the easier win, the mid-day re-plan is where it gets interesting.

So if I play that back. 420 trucks, three terminals, routes built manually every night in spreadsheets, overtime at fourteen percent of driver hours against a target of six, and about forty k a month in chargebacks. Plus the hours-of-service risk, which is more of a safety and compliance thing. Did I miss anything?
No, that's — when you say it out loud it's kind of bleak. There's one more, the customer calls, but let's park that. Elena's going to want to talk about systems before I get on my soapbox.
Ha. Fair. Let's park it, I wrote it down. What would good look like for you, though? Like, if we're sitting here in six months and this worked, what's different?

Honestly? Dispatchers go home at seven. Overtime under eight percent. Chargebacks cut in half, so call it twenty k a month instead of forty. If I could walk into Dana's office with that, I don't have to sell anything internally. It sells itself.
That's a really clear bar. I like that a lot. It's measurable, too, which makes my life easier. Have you tried to fix this before? Like, is there a routing tool that came and went?

Ha. Yes. So about four years ago, before my time actually, they bought a routing add-on that came bundled with the TMS. Oracle had a module. It ran overnight, it spat out routes, and the dispatchers looked at them and said these are garbage, and went back to Excel within like a month. And to be fair to the dispatchers, the routes were garbage. It didn't know anything about dock times, it didn't know a driver's hours, it just did shortest path. So there's a little bit of scar tissue on the floor. When I say routing software to my leads, the first face they make is not a happy face.
That's really good to know. So adoption with the dispatchers is its own thing we'd need to earn.
A hundred percent. If my Kent lead, Ray, doesn't buy in, it doesn't matter what I sign. He'll just quietly keep the spreadsheet open on his second monitor. I would, too, honestly, if I were him.

That's actually one of the things we designed around. Dispatchers can override anything the engine does, drag a stop, lock a route, and it'll re-plan around what they locked instead of fighting them. It's meant to feel like a really fast assistant, not an autopilot. But again, better to show than tell. Thursday or whenever we do the demo, it'd be great if Ray could be on.
Maybe. Let me see. He's not a big Zoom guy. But if I can get him to watch the recording, that might be enough.
Elena, over to you. What does the landscape look like on your side?

Okay. So, telematics is Samsara. All 420 trucks have Samsara units, we've been on them about three years. That part is fine, it's modern, there's an API, we already pull GPS and hours of service from it into a couple of internal dashboards. The problem is the TMS. We're on Oracle Transportation Management, on-prem, and the version is from 2014. It's heavily customized. Nobody who customized it still works here.
Ah. The classic.

Yes. Very classic. So the orders live there. Customer appointments live there. Rates live there. And there is no real API. There are some database views that I'm allowed to read, and there's a batch export that runs every night for finance. That's it. Upgrading it is a separate project, and that project is not funded, so please don't tell me the answer is upgrade the TMS.
Ha, noted. Do the dispatchers export from the TMS into the spreadsheets today?
Yes. Every afternoon, the export lands on a shared drive, someone pastes it into the template. Sometimes the wrong day's file. That has also happened.
We don't talk about that week.

Okay, so, I won't pretend to be the right person for the deep integration question. That's exactly why I want Daniel on the next call. He's our staff engineer, he's built most of our integrations. But at a high level, we already have a Samsara integration, it's live with a number of our customers. And for the TMS side we've done file-based integrations before, so it's not a new problem for us.
Which customers on Oracle on-prem?

Uh, that's a — I'd want to check which ones are specifically Oracle. I know we've done older on-prem TMS setups, there's a parcel fleet in Ohio on some ancient system, I don't remember which one off the top of my head. I'll get you a straight answer on that instead of guessing.
Please. Because I have heard 'we've done file-based integrations' from three vendors now and every time it turns out to be a CSV upload button in the UI and a person whose job is to click it.

That's fair. And for what it's worth, there's a real difference between someone uploading a CSV once a day and a scheduled pull with validation and error handling and alerting when the file doesn't show up. Daniel can walk you through what it actually looks like. I'd rather he show you than we describe it.
Okay. Good. I'll also want to know what happens when an order changes in the TMS after the export. Because that happens constantly.
Yeah, that's a good one. Is the change rate high? Like, how many orders get modified after the nightly cutoff?
I don't have a precise number. Marcus?

Ten percent? Maybe more in peak. Appointment changes mostly. A DC calls and moves a slot, or a customer adds a pallet. The dispatchers find out by phone and then somebody updates the TMS later. Sometimes much later.

So the TMS is not always the source of truth, is what he's saying. Which is a problem for any integration, not just yours. I just want to be clear about it up front so nobody acts surprised in the pilot.
No, that's really helpful. And on the network side, can anything talk to that box from the outside, or is it locked down?

Locked down. Nothing inbound. We can push files outbound over SFTP, that's how we do the finance export to our accounting provider. Anything that needs a connection into the data center goes through a change board, and the change board meets once a month, and they are not fast people.

Got it. So outbound SFTP is possible today, inbound is a change board. That's a good thing for Daniel to know before Thursday, or, sorry, before the demo, whenever we land it. Okay. Writing all that down. What else is on your list? Security, SSO?

Yes. So, SSO is Okta. Anything new has to be behind Okta, no exceptions, our CISO is very clear about that. SAML is fine. SCIM for provisioning would be nice, it's not a hard requirement. Then security review. I'll need your SOC 2 report, Type II, and we have a security questionnaire. It's, I think, about 180 questions. I'm sorry in advance.
No, that's totally normal. We're SOC 2 Type II, I can get you the report under NDA this week. And the questionnaire, send it over, we have folks who turn those around.

And roles. We'd need at least three. Dispatchers, terminal leads, and a read-only role for customer service. We manage all of that in Okta groups, so I'd want the roles to come from the group, not be set by hand in your admin screen by whoever remembers to do it.

Yep, we map roles from SAML group claims, so that works the way you'd want. I'll double check on SCIM, I believe it's supported on the enterprise plan, but I'd rather confirm than say yes and be wrong.
Okay. And the questionnaire, how long does it usually take you?
Usually about a week, a week and a half for one that size.
Hm. Okay. If it's a week and a half that's fine. If it's a month, that's the decision date, so.
No, understood. We'll prioritize it. I'll make sure it doesn't become the long pole.
Okay. And data. Where is the data hosted, and does any of our customer data go to third parties? Like, are you sending our stops to some mapping provider?

We're hosted in AWS, US regions. We do use a third-party map data provider for the road network and traffic. Addresses and coordinates go to it for routing, no customer names, no order details. That'll all be in the questionnaire answers and the subprocessor list, but I want you to hear it now and not be surprised by it later.
Okay. I appreciate that. That's the kind of thing that usually comes up in week five.
Elena's killed two vendors in week five.
They deserved it.
Ha. Noted. We'll try very hard not to be the third.
So let me switch gears a little. Marcus, if this goes well, how does a decision actually get made at Harbor & Pine? Who else needs to be involved?

So, I own operations. I'm the one who's going to live with it and I'm the one pushing for it. But anything at this size goes to Dana. Dana Whitfield, our CFO. She signs off, and honestly she's the one I have to convince. She's not anti, she's just, she's been burned. We bought a yard management thing two years ago that was supposed to save us a fortune, and we turned it off after eight months. She brings it up. Not often. But she brings it up.
Got it. What would Dana need to see?

Numbers on our trucks. Not your case study, not a nice slide about some grocery fleet in Ohio. She'll want a pilot. We want a pilot, frankly. Run it on a chunk of the fleet, show me the miles, show me overtime, show me late deliveries on those routes, and then we talk.
That makes total sense. And timing, is there a date you're working toward?

October 30th. We want a decision by the end of October. Dana does the budget for next year in November, and if it's not in by then, it's basically next fiscal year, and I really don't want to go through another peak like this one.
Okay, October 30. That's tight with a pilot in there, but doable if we move this week.
It's tight, I know. I'd rather it be tight.

Just thinking out loud. If the decision is October 30, the pilot can't be a full quarter. We'd need something that shows real signal in, what, four weeks? Can you get Dana a read on overtime in four weeks?

Overtime, yes, that's weekly payroll, it shows up fast. Chargebacks lag. They come in thirty to forty-five days after the delivery. So we'd see overtime and on-time pretty quick, and then chargebacks we'd have to kind of project.
Okay, that's useful. On-time at the DC appointment is a pretty good leading indicator for chargebacks. We could make that the headline metric and project the dollars off it.
And budget, I'll just ask directly. Is there budget set aside for this, or is this something that has to be carved out?

So, I'll be candid. I've got a number in my head and I've talked to Dana about the range. Something in the neighborhood of three hundred k a year is, um, it's not crazy to us. If the numbers hold. If you come in and the pilot shows we save half the overtime and half the chargebacks, that's well over three hundred, and it's an easy conversation. If the pilot's mushy, three hundred k is a very hard conversation and I'm the guy who brought it in.
That's fair, and honestly that's the right way to buy this. For context, at 420 trucks we'd land right around there, a little over at list, depending on terms.
Yeah. And look, I'll be straight with you about the other thing too, since you're going to ask anyway. We're talking to RouteWise.
Sure. I figured you might be.
Their number came in around fifty-two dollars a truck a month. So, that's cheaper. Noticeably cheaper.
Yeah. What do you like about them so far, other than that?

Price. Honestly, it's mostly price. The demo was fine. It felt a bit, like, older? The dispatch screen looked like our spreadsheets with a nicer font. But they did say they have an Oracle connector, which got Elena's attention.
It got my attention. It did not get my trust. I asked if it was certified for our version and they said they would follow up. That was two weeks ago.

Got it. Look, I won't trash them, they're a real company and they've got customers. What I'd say is, the price per truck isn't the number Dana's going to care about. It's what the routes save. Our beta fleets on the new engine, Routing v3, are seeing about eleven percent fewer miles driven, and on-time going from ninety-one to almost ninety-five percent. If that holds on your fleet, a few dollars a truck is kind of a rounding error.
If it holds. Everybody's beta is great.

That's fair. That's exactly what the pilot's for. But let me just do the napkin math out loud, and correct me where I'm off. Forty k a month in chargebacks is call it four hundred and eighty k a year. If we take half of that, that's two-forty. Then overtime. I don't know your payroll, but if you've got, what, four-hundred-some drivers and fourteen percent of their hours are at time and a half, going from fourteen to eight is a big number. Probably bigger than the chargebacks. So against three hundred k, the math works pretty fast, even if we only hit half of what you said good looks like.
Yeah. I've done that napkin too. It's why I'm on this call. But Dana doesn't buy napkins. She buys the spreadsheet with our payroll in it.

Totally. And that's the one we'll build together, with your numbers. I'm just saying the gap between us and RouteWise is about sixteen bucks a truck, and the thing you're trying to fix is a lot bigger than sixteen bucks a truck.

Ha. Okay. I'll give you that one. For now. So, the criteria. I'll tell you how I'd frame it for Dana. One, does it actually cut overtime and late deliveries on our trucks. Two, can Elena integrate it without a six-month project. Three, does it pass security. And four, price. Price is fourth, but it's on the list, I'm not going to pretend it isn't.
That's super helpful. Elena, would you add anything?
Only that the integration is a gate, not a score. If it doesn't work with the TMS, it does not matter how good the routes are.
Understood. Gate, not a score. I'll use that. And on the paper side, once Dana says yes, what does that look like? Legal, procurement, anything we should know about?

So, we don't have a procurement team, really. It's me, Dana, and our outside counsel looks at the MSA. They're not slow, but they're not free either, so Dana likes it when vendors use reasonable paper. Last time it took about two weeks from yes to signature. And Elena's security sign-off has to be done before legal will even open it.
That's correct. Security first, then legal. Not in parallel. I've asked.
Okay, that's important. So if we're working back from October 30, security review has to basically be done by the time the pilot's wrapping up. Which means the questionnaire needs to start this week.
Yeah. That's the critical path, honestly. Not the pilot.
And for the pilot itself, I'm thinking out loud, but would you want it on one terminal or spread across all three? Like, a chunk of Kent?

Kent, probably. It's the biggest, it's got the worst chargeback accounts, and Ray's there, so if it works there it works anywhere. Fifty, sixty trucks maybe. I don't want to bet the whole terminal on a pilot in peak. Dana would kill me.

Fifty or sixty trucks in Kent. That's a really sensible size. Let me take that back and we'll put together something concrete on what a pilot looks like, including how we'd measure it, so Dana's not looking at our numbers, she's looking at yours.
That would help a lot. If the measurement is my payroll data and my on-time data, she'll trust it. If it's your dashboard she'll assume it's marketing.
Okay. Can I get on my soapbox now?
Please. The customer calls.

The customer calls. So, our retail customers, and some of the industrial ones too, they keep calling dispatchers asking where's my truck. All day. My dispatchers, the same people who are supposed to be fixing the plan when something breaks, spend I'd say a third of their day on the phone telling a receiving manager at a DC that the truck is twenty minutes out. And half the time they're guessing, because they're looking at a dot on the Samsara map and doing math in their head. So what I really want is something where the customer gets a link, they see the truck, they see a real ETA, and they stop calling us. Is that something you do? Live ETA sharing, tracking link, whatever you call it.
Yeah, so, that's on the roadmap for this quarter. It's something we're actively working on, and honestly it's one of the things I'm most excited about, because we hear it from a lot of fleets.
This quarter, like, by the end of the year?
That's the plan, yeah.

Yeah, I, um. Just to be precise about where it is. We're scoping it now. The ETA piece underneath it is real, it's the same model that's in the new routing engine, and it's gotten a lot more accurate this year. But the customer-facing link itself, I don't want to give you a date on this call and then have to walk it back in three weeks. Let me come back to you with something firmer.

Okay. I appreciate that. I'm just going to be honest, that one's a must-have for us. Not a nice-to-have. If I go to Dana and say we cut overtime but the dispatchers are still on the phone all day, half the value is gone. And the customers who call the most are the same ones charging us back.
Totally hear you. And it's the right priority. We'll make sure you have a clear picture of it well before the pilot decision.
And if it exists, it has to work off the Samsara GPS, not some separate app on the driver's phone. We are not putting another app on 420 phones. The drivers already hate the one they have.
Yep, understood. That's a really good constraint to know now.

And just so you know the size of it. I had one of my leads tally calls for a week in August. Kent alone, about three hundred and forty inbound where's-my-truck calls. In a week. That's one terminal. So it's not a little feature for us. It's probably a full dispatcher's worth of time, maybe two.
That's a great stat. Can I use that with our product team? It really helps make the case internally.
Use it. Please. Make the case. I'd rather you build it than RouteWise does.
That's really helpful, genuinely. That kind of number moves things up a list. I'll take it back.
Okay. Good.

So, next steps. Here's what I'd propose. Thursday, October 1st, we do a real demo. I'll bring Daniel, our staff engineer. He'll show you Routing v3, the dispatch board, re-planning when a truck goes down, and he can go deep with Elena on Samsara and the TMS question. Does Thursday work?
Thursday. What time are you thinking?
How about eleven Pacific? I'll book forty-five minutes in case Elena has a lot of questions.
I will have a lot of questions.
Eleven works. I'll move a thing.

Great. On my side, I'll send the SOC 2 report under NDA today or tomorrow. Elena, if you can send over the security questionnaire, I'll get our team started on it right away. And I'll find out about Oracle on-prem references.
I'll send the questionnaire after this call. And the TMS version details and a sample of the nightly export, so Daniel can look at it before Thursday.
Perfect, that'd be really helpful.
And Marcus, if you could share one night's routes, even just one terminal, anonymized is fine, we can run it through the engine before Thursday so the demo's on your network and not some fake city.
Oh, that'd be great actually. I can get you Kent from last Tuesday. That was a bad night, so it's a good test.
Even better. And Marcus, is it worth looping Dana in at any point before the pilot? Even fifteen minutes?
Not yet. Let me brief her after Thursday. If I bring her in too early she'll ask for the ROI model and we don't have it yet. Once I've seen the demo I'll know what I'm actually pitching.

Makes sense. Okay, let me just recap so we're all on the same page, and then I'll let you go. Thursday at eleven Pacific, Routing v3 demo with Daniel, ideally on your Kent data from last Tuesday. Before that, I send the SOC 2 report under NDA, Elena sends the questionnaire, the TMS version and a sample export, and I come back on Oracle on-prem references. After Thursday, Marcus briefs Dana, and we put together a pilot proposal, fifty to sixty trucks in Kent, measured on your payroll and on-time data, so you can make a decision by October 30. And on live ETA, we owe you something firmer. Did I miss anything?
SCIM. Asher said he'd confirm.
Yes, SCIM. On me.
Perfect. Thank you both, this was really, really useful.
Yeah, thanks guys. Good call.
Thank you. Talk Thursday.
Thanks, see you Thursday.

general.tldr: Harbor & Pine (420 trucks) has strong, quantified pain: 14% overtime and ~$40k/month in chargebacks. CFO Dana Whitfield decides by Oct 30 after a pilot, RouteWise is cheaper at ~$52/truck, and Marcus calls live ETA sharing a must-have, which Tom placed on 'this quarter's' roadmap before Asher hedged.

items.text: Discovery with Marcus Hill (Director of Ops) and Elena Petrova (IT & Integrations): understand dispatch today, systems constraints and how Harbor & Pine will buy. No demo, by design.
Nine dispatchers and two leads hand-build routes in Excel every night for 420 trucks across Kent, Portland and Spokane, often until 10–11 p.m.
Overtime is ~14% of driver hours against a 6% budget, up from 11% in the spring; late-delivery chargebacks run ~$40k/month.
Success bar from Marcus: dispatchers home by 7, overtime under 8%, chargebacks cut in half.
CFO Dana Whitfield signs off; she wants a pilot on H&P's own trucks and a decision by Oct 30, ahead of November budgeting.
Budget is around $300k/yr 'if the numbers hold'. RouteWise quoted ~$52/truck/month.
Live ETA sharing is a must-have. Tom said it is 'on the roadmap for this quarter'; Asher corrected that it is still being scoped and declined to give a date.
Mid-day re-planning is done by gut: the terminal lead calls the nearest driver, who picks up extra stops and runs into overtime.
Drivers hit hours-of-service limits with freight on board three times in August (Elena's correction of Marcus's 'twice').
Marcus guesses chargebacks split about half bad plans, half failed same-day re-plans; he has no hard data.
A bundled Oracle routing module failed about four years ago, so dispatchers are wary. Adoption depends on Kent lead Ray.
Samsara telematics on all 420 trucks, with a usable API. Oracle TMS is on-prem, from 2014, heavily customized, with no API; an upgrade is not funded.
Only outbound SFTP is possible today. Any inbound connection needs a monthly change board.
About 10% of orders change after the nightly cutoff, so the TMS is not always the source of truth.
Requirements: Okta SSO (SAML), roles mapped from Okta groups, SCIM nice-to-have, SOC 2 Type II report and a ~180-question security questionnaire.
Elena is skeptical of 'file-based integration' claims and asked for Oracle on-prem references. Tom could not name one on the call.
Dispatchers spend about a third of their day on 'where's my truck' calls; Kent logged ~340 such calls in one August week.
Elena: it must run off Samsara GPS, not a new driver app on 420 phones.
Tom's 'this quarter' framing is a commitment risk. Asher said only that Tandem is scoping it and owes Marcus something firmer.
Routing v3 demo with Daniel on Thu Oct 1, 11:00 PT, ideally on Kent route data.

highlights.title: Marcus quantifies the pain: 14% overtime, $40k/month chargebacks
Dana Whitfield signs off; pilot first, decision by Oct 30
RouteWise at $52/truck; Elena doesn't trust their Oracle connector
Tom puts live ETA on 'this quarter's' roadmap; Asher hedges

ask.q: What did we say about live ETA?
ask.a: When Marcus asked for a customer-facing tracking link, Tom said live ETA sharing is 'on the roadmap for this quarter' and confirmed 'that's the plan' for end of year. Asher stepped in to say Tandem is still scoping it and would not give a date, promising something firmer. Marcus called it a must-have, and Elena said it has to run off Samsara GPS, not a new driver app.

Dana Whitfield, Harbor & Pine's CFO. She signs off on anything this size and was burned by a yard management tool that was shut off after eight months, so she wants pilot results on H&P's own trucks. She hasn't been on a call; Marcus will brief her after the Oct 1 demo.

Marcus ranked them: cuts overtime and late deliveries on H&P's trucks, integrates without a six-month project, passes security, and then price. Elena added that the Oracle TMS integration is a pass/fail gate, not a weighted score. Live ETA sharing was also called a must-have.

ask.q: How do we compare to RouteWise?
ask.a: RouteWise quoted about $52/truck/month, which is cheaper, and Marcus says price is mostly what he likes about them. Their UI felt dated, and their claimed Oracle connector is unproven: two weeks on, they haven't confirmed support for H&P's version. Tom framed the ~$16/truck gap against Routing v3's beta results (11% fewer miles, on-time 91% to almost 95%) and the scale of H&P's overtime and chargeback costs.

Samsara is modern and has an API. The Oracle TMS is a heavily customized 2014 on-prem install with no API, only readable database views and a nightly batch export. Nothing inbound is allowed without a monthly change board, but outbound SFTP works today. About 10% of orders change after the nightly cutoff.

ask.q: What does success look like for Harbor & Pine?
ask.a: Dispatchers home by 7 p.m., overtime under 8% of driver hours (from ~14%) and chargebacks halved from ~$40k/month to ~$20k. The pilot will lead with on-time at DC appointments, because chargebacks show up 30–45 days late.
